title: GOD FORBADE A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER—BUT THE REASON GOES DEEPER THAN SEX
paragraphs: GOD FORBADE A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH A WOMAN AND HER DAUGHTER—BUT THE REASON GOES DEEPER THAN SEX

Leviticus 18:17 reveals a disturbing truth about lust, family betrayal, and the sacred boundaries God established to protect human dignity. And when we follow this uncomfortable Scripture all the way to Jesus Christ, we discover something even more powerful: the God who exposes sin is also the God who offers redemption.
There are sins that destroy a marriage.
There are sins that destroy a family.
And then there are sins that make a daughter look at her own mother and wonder whether she was ever truly safe.
Imagine a woman discovering that the man she trusted, the man who shared her bed, her secrets, and perhaps her home, had also pursued her daughter.
Imagine the silence at the dinner table.
The unbearable questions.
The daughter wondering whether she had somehow caused it. The mother struggling between heartbreak and disbelief. The family relationships that may never feel the same again.
Now imagine opening the Bible and discovering that thousands of years ago, God had already spoken directly against this kind of sexual wrongdoing.
Not because He hated intimacy.
Not because He considered sexuality dirty.
But because He knew that human desire, when separated from holiness and love, could become an instrument of devastating betrayal.
And the most astonishing part?
The Hebrew text contains a word that exposes the seriousness of this sin with remarkable force.
Listen carefully to what God actually said.
Leviticus 18:17 declares in the King James Version:

“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.”
That final word deserves our attention.
Because God was not merely establishing an ancient social custom.
He was identifying a violation of family boundaries so serious that His covenant people were forbidden to normalize it.
And to understand why, we must enter the world of the text rather than force the text into the world of our assumptions.
The original Hebrew begins:
עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
ʿErvat ʾishshah u-vittah lo tegalleh.
Literally, the phrase means:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter.”
The expression “uncover nakedness” is not simply about seeing someone without clothing. Within Leviticus 18, it is a Hebrew expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
The verb תְגַלֵּה (tegalleh) comes from the root גלה (galah), meaning to uncover or reveal.
The noun עֶרְוָה (ʿervah) refers to nakedness and, in this legal context, sexual exposure.
God was not discussing an accidental glance.
He was prohibiting sexual involvement that crossed forbidden family boundaries.

The verse also extends the prohibition to a woman's granddaughter through either her son or her daughter. The issue is therefore broader than one specific mother-daughter relationship. It concerns sexual relationships involving closely connected generations of the same family.
Then comes the explanation:
שַׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה
Sheʾarah hennah.
“They are her close relatives.”
The Hebrew emphasizes their familial connection.
These women are not unrelated individuals whose relationships can be considered in isolation. They belong to an interconnected family structure.
A sexual relationship with one cannot be morally separated from the consequences of involving another in that same forbidden union.
And then Scripture delivers its verdict:
זִמָּה הִוא
Zimmah hi.
“It is wickedness.”
The Hebrew noun זִמָּה (zimmah) can describe wickedness, depravity, or an evil sexual scheme, depending on context.
Here, it condemns the prohibited relationship as a serious moral wrong.
Notice something important.

The Hebrew text does not explicitly say that the prohibition was given because the daughter would become jealous, because the mother would be emotionally devastated, or because the family would suffer psychological trauma.
Those consequences may be very real.
But we must distinguish what Scripture explicitly teaches from the reasonable moral implications we draw from it.
The stated reason in Leviticus 18:17 is the close family relationship, and the act is condemned as wickedness.
That distinction matters.
Because we do not honor God's Word by making it say more than it says.
We honor His Word by listening carefully enough to hear what He actually revealed.
And what He revealed is already serious enough.
The God of Israel did not permit sexual desire to erase the boundaries of kinship.
A man could not simply claim that because he desired someone, he had a right to pursue her.
Desire was never meant to become the final authority over righteousness.
And that truth is just as relevant today.
We live in a world where people sometimes defend destructive relationships with phrases that sound compassionate.
“We love each other.”
“Nobody understands our connection.”
“We never intended to hurt anyone.”
“It's complicated.”
But sincerity does not automatically make a relationship holy.
Strong feelings do not turn a forbidden act into an acceptable one.
And secrecy does not make betrayal disappear.
Some relationships are wrong not because the emotions involved are necessarily imaginary, but because the actions violate obligations and boundaries that love itself should respect.
That is part of the moral force of Leviticus 18.
God does not ask merely whether something is desired.
He asks whether it is righteous.
And the difference between those questions can change an entire life.
Consider the setting.
Leviticus 18 was given to Israel as part of God's covenant instruction after the exodus from Egypt.
The chapter opens with a command that establishes the larger issue.
God tells Israel not to imitate the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or Canaan, where they were going.
Instead, they were to walk according to His statutes.
Then comes Leviticus 18:5:
“Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD.”
This chapter is not an isolated collection of strange ancient restrictions.
It belongs to a larger biblical vision of holiness.
God was forming a people who were to be different from the nations around them.
Their worship mattered.
Their treatment of others mattered.
Their sexual conduct mattered.
Their family relationships mattered.
Holiness was never meant to exist only inside a place of worship while injustice and exploitation flourished behind closed doors.
And that should trouble anyone who has learned to appear righteous in public while concealing destructive behavior in private.
Because the God who said, “I am the LORD,” was claiming authority over the whole life of His people.
Not merely their ceremonies.
Not merely their sacrifices.
Not merely the words they spoke when others were listening.
Their lives.
Their bodies.
Their relationships.
Their conduct when no human witness was present.
And perhaps that is where this passage begins to feel uncomfortably personal.
Because although most readers may never have committed the specific act prohibited in Leviticus 18:17, many understand the temptation to excuse something they know is wrong.
The private conversation that should have ended.
The flirtation that crossed a boundary.
The hidden messages.
The emotional attachment that became more important than a marriage covenant.
The secret someone keeps protecting because admitting the truth would require repentance.
Not every temptation is the same as the offense described in Leviticus.
And we must never pretend that all sexual sins have identical consequences.
But there is a common spiritual danger.
When desire becomes our master, we begin negotiating with boundaries that once seemed obvious.
We stop asking, “What does God say?”
And start asking, “How far can I go without anyone finding out?”
That is a dangerous question.
Because a hidden sin can become a public wound long before it becomes a public scandal.
And God cares about the people who are wounded.
Think about the daughter.

In situations involving coercion, manipulation, or abuse, especially when the daughter is a minor or the man occupies a position of parental authority, the wrongdoing can include a profound betrayal of trust and responsibility.
A child cannot be held responsible for an adult's sexual exploitation.
A person who is coerced or abused is not guilty merely because someone violated them.
This distinction is essential.
Leviticus 18:17 identifies a prohibited sexual relationship. It must never be twisted into a weapon for blaming victims or silencing those who have been harmed.
Scripture consistently calls God's people to oppose injustice and protect the vulnerable.
Psalm 82:3–4 commands:
“Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked.”
God's concern for holiness does not cancel His concern for the wounded.
It includes it.
And if someone has used religious language to pressure you into silence about abuse, that pressure should not be confused with biblical faithfulness.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
Justice matters.
And forgiveness does not require a victim to return to danger, conceal a crime, or pretend that trust has already been restored.
That is not rebellion against grace.
That is taking evil seriously.
But there is another question that must be answered.
Why would God prohibit sexual relationships involving a woman and her daughter when the Bible itself records troubling family arrangements among people in earlier generations?
For example, Jacob married both Leah and Rachel, who were sisters, as recorded in Genesis 29.
Later, Leviticus 18:18 specifically prohibited taking a wife's sister as a rival wife while the first wife was living.
The Bible also records instances of polygamy and other deeply complicated family arrangements.
Does that mean God changed His mind about holiness?
Not necessarily.
We must distinguish between Scripture describing what people did and Scripture approving what they did.
A historical account is not automatically a moral endorsement.
Genesis often shows the painful consequences of human choices without interrupting every narrative to provide a formal legal judgment.
Jacob's household, for example, was marked by rivalry, jealousy, and deep family conflict.
The existence of a practice in biblical history does not prove that the practice represents God's ideal.
And when Jesus was questioned about marriage and divorce, He directed His listeners back to God's creation design.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus referred to the creation of male and female and the union in which husband and wife become one flesh.
He did not present marriage as an arrangement where human appetite could override covenant faithfulness.
He called attention to what God had joined together.
That is where the larger biblical story begins to come into focus.
The Bible does not treat sexuality as meaningless.
It treats it as powerful.
Powerful enough to create life.
Powerful enough to express covenant intimacy.
Powerful enough, when misused, to inflict lasting harm.
The answer to destructive sexuality is not to despise the human body.
The answer is to recover the holiness of love.
Love does not ask how many boundaries it can cross.
Love asks how faithfully it can honor God and protect another person's dignity.
And this is where the story takes a turn that some readers may not expect.
Because the Bible does not end with Leviticus.
And the God who exposes wickedness does not leave repentant sinners without hope.
Centuries after Moses, Jesus Christ stood before a world filled with broken families, hidden shame, sexual wrongdoing, hypocrisy, and wounded people.
He did not come to declare that sin was harmless.
He came to save sinners.
John 1:14 tells us that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And we see that combination powerfully in John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
He knows the painful complexity of her relationship history.
He tells her that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
Yet He does not reduce her entire identity to her history.
He speaks with her.
He reveals Himself to her.
He offers living water.
And she becomes a witness to others, inviting her community to come and see the One who knew her life.
We should be careful not to invent details about this woman that Scripture does not provide.
The text does not tell us why each marriage ended, whether she was responsible for those endings, or whether she had been abandoned or mistreated.
What it does show is extraordinary.
Jesus knew the truth about her life.
And He still engaged her with dignity.
He did not need to deny reality in order to offer hope.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Christ does not save us by pretending sin is not sin.
He saves by confronting the reality of our condition and offering the grace we could never earn.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had perfected our image.
Not after everyone had forgotten our failures.
Not after we had finally become impressive enough to deserve His attention.
Christ died for sinners.
But grace is not permission to continue harming others.
The same Gospel that offers forgiveness also calls us to repentance.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It means to repent, involving a change of mind and direction.
In biblical usage, repentance is more than temporary regret or embarrassment over being caught.
It is a turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Jesus said in Mark 1:15:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Repent.
Believe.
Not conceal.
Not rationalize.
Not blame the wounded.
Not demand immediate forgiveness from people who are still struggling to recover from what happened.
Repentance takes responsibility.

And where serious harm has occurred, genuine repentance may involve confession, ending the wrongdoing, accepting appropriate consequences, making restitution where possible, and respecting the safety and boundaries of those affected.
Forgiveness before God is not a license to escape earthly accountability.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant abuse.
It is God's invitation to leave darkness and walk in the light.
Perhaps someone reading this has been living with a secret.
Perhaps it is not the specific sin named in Leviticus 18:17.
Perhaps it is a betrayal that has been eating away at your conscience.
Perhaps you have spent years defending something God has been asking you to surrender.
You can convince other people that everything is fine.
You can create a convincing explanation.
You can even become skilled at quoting Scripture while avoiding the one passage that confronts your behavior.
But you cannot heal a wound by insisting it does not exist.
And you cannot build a transformed life while remaining determined to protect the very thing that is destroying it.
There is hope.
Not because the wrongdoing was small.
But because the mercy of Jesus Christ is great.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice that the promise does not require us to call darkness light.
It invites us to confess.
To stop defending what God condemns.
To stop treating our desires as unquestionable authorities.
To come into the light.
And to trust the Savior whose blood was shed for sinners.
But perhaps you are not the person who committed the betrayal.
Perhaps you are the person who suffered because of it.
Perhaps someone who should have protected you crossed a boundary that should never have been crossed.
Perhaps your family demanded silence to preserve its reputation.
Perhaps you were told that speaking about what happened would dishonor God.
Hear this carefully.
The shame of another person's wrongdoing does not belong to you.
You do not have to carry the moral guilt of someone who exploited, manipulated, or violated you.
And you do not have to call something acceptable simply because it happened inside a religious household.
The Lord sees what people conceal.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
God's nearness does not mean every wound disappears overnight.
Healing can take time.
It can involve grief, trustworthy support, professional care, difficult boundaries, and the slow rebuilding of a sense of safety.
But your suffering does not make you invisible to Him.
And the cross of Jesus Christ is not a demand that you deny what happened.
It is the revelation of a Savior who entered a world of evil and suffering to overcome sin and death.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the repentant sinner.
And there is room at the feet of Jesus for the wounded person who is still learning how to breathe again.
These are not identical situations.
They should never be treated as though they are.
But both reveal how desperately humanity needs a Savior.
That brings us back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Why did the Old Testament forbid sexual relations with a woman and her daughter?
Because God established boundaries around close family relationships and explicitly condemned this kind of sexual union as wickedness.
Because holiness includes what people do with their bodies, not merely what they profess with their lips.
Because sexual desire does not have the authority to overturn God's moral instruction.
And because, when we read this command within the whole counsel of Scripture, we recognize that God calls His people to faithfulness, self-control, justice, and love that refuses to exploit others.

The specific prohibition was given within Israel's covenant law, but Christians do not need to pretend that every provision of the Mosaic law functions identically under the new covenant in order to recognize its moral seriousness.
The New Testament continues to condemn sexual immorality and calls believers to honor God with their bodies.
First Corinthians 6:18–20 speaks of fleeing sexual immorality and remembering that believers belong to God.
The Christian response, therefore, is not simply to memorize an ancient prohibition.
It is to surrender the whole life to Jesus Christ.
To allow His truth to confront our excuses.
To allow His grace to break the power of shame.
To allow His Spirit to cultivate holiness, faithfulness, and self-control.
And to remember that the purpose of the Gospel is not merely to produce people who look respectable.
It is to reconcile sinners to God through Christ and transform them into people who increasingly reflect His character.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior will never be that your scandal is greater than the cross.
But neither will we tell you that the cross makes your sin insignificant.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable with the darkness.
He gave Himself to redeem us.
Titus 2:14 says that Christ “gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.”
Redeem.
Purify.
Transform.
That is the Gospel's direction.
From bondage toward freedom.
From deception toward truth.
From rebellion toward repentance.
From shame toward the grace of God.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by erasing the reality of the past.
Not by declaring every consequence canceled.
But by making a genuinely new life possible through His death and resurrection.
And perhaps that is why you needed to encounter this difficult passage today.
Not to satisfy curiosity about an ancient sexual prohibition.
But to remember that God cares about what happens behind closed doors.
He cares about the vulnerable.
He cares about truth.
He cares about the person whose conscience has been warning them to turn back.
And He cares about the person who has been carrying a wound no one else seems willing to acknowledge.
If this article has confronted something in your life, I invite you to respond with sincerity rather than performance.
You do not need to disclose intimate details, name anyone involved, or expose private trauma in a public comment.
God already knows the parts of your story that you are not ready to tell the world.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ has brought you from darkness into a changed life, your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that transformation is impossible.

Not because every person needs to know your private struggles, but because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the difference between love and lust, between guilt and repentance, or between religious appearances and genuine holiness.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people who have grown distant from church, and even those who are still searching for faith to follow along.
Because God's Word deserves to be studied carefully, not merely quoted dramatically.
And because the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be heard beyond the walls of a church building.
Some believers prayerfully include support for Gospel-centered ministries as part of their regular giving. If you choose to do that here, we receive it with gratitude as a ministry offering.
But I want to be clear about something important.
You do not have to pay for God's forgiveness.
You do not have to give money to prove your faith.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, not something purchased through religious support.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible, including to those who cannot afford to contribute financially.
Not everyone can give financially.
But everyone who belongs to Christ has opportunities to bear witness to Him.
And that is what matters most.
Not our popularity.
Jesus Christ.
His truth.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His grace.
His power to redeem and transform.
Because one day, the arguments we used to justify our sin will no longer matter.
The reputation we worked so hard to preserve will no longer save us.
The secrets we kept will not become righteous simply because they remained undiscovered.
What matters eternally is whether we have turned to the Savior who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Leviticus 18:17 reminds us that God does not overlook evil simply because it happens inside a family.
The Gospel reminds us that evil does not have to be the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And that is a truth worth remembering.
Worth living.
Worth sharing.
The most powerful ending to a scandal is not when the world finally stops talking about it, but when a life truly surrendered to Jesus begins telling a different story.
